# Hierarchical Depth Map Rendering

Also called: Hierarchical Z-Buffer Rendering, Hierarchical model with multi-layered depth images

## Overview
Hierarchical Depth Map Rendering is an image-based rendering technique that combines a hierarchical geometric model with precomputed multi-layer depth images to efficiently render complex vegetation [S2, book]. It differs from sibling methods by resampling precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images of hierarchical plant subparts rather than rendering geometry directly or using generic point clouds [S2, book]. The method builds on [Depth Map Rendering and Visualization](8160-depth-map-rendering-and-visualization.md) and is designed for offline or precomputed scenarios, as it is not real-time [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
*   **Inputs:** Hierarchical model with precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images and a new viewpoint location [S2, book].
*   **Outputs:** Antialiased color image [S2, book].

**Data Structures:**
The core data structure is a multi-layer z-buffer [S2, book]. Each layer contains the following fields [S2, book]:
1.  **Surface Normal:** 3D vector [S2, book].
2.  **Surface Diffuse Reflectivity Color:** 3D vector [S2, book].
3.  **Subpixel Coverage Mask:** Coverage mask [S2, book].
4.  **Z Value:** Depth value [S2, book].
5.  **Leaf Bit:** Boolean flag indicating if the surface is a leaf [S2, book].

**Numbered Steps:**
1.  **Subpart Selection:** Determine which subparts to render based on viewpoint distance [S2, book]. Parts closer to the viewpoint use higher-detail images from deeper levels of the hierarchical model [S2, book]. The closest parts are scan-converted directly from the original texture/transparency mapped polygons [S2, book].
2.  **Resampling:** Resample the precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images of the selected hierarchical subparts to the new viewpoint [S2, book].
3.  **Shading:** Perform shading as a post-process on the resampled z-buffer layers [S2, book]. Apply a z-buffer shadow algorithm to determine if surface points are in shadow [S2, book]. If not in shadow, add the effect of unattenuated direct sunlight using the Phong [BRDF](#14809-bidirectional-reflectance-distribution-function-brdf.md) for a discrete parallel light source [S2, book]. If the **Leaf Bit** is set, include diffusely transmitted light from the back of the leaf [S2, book].
4.  **[Compositing](#2436-compositing.md):** Composite the shading results from all layers into an antialiased color value for each pixel using the subpixel coverage masks, following the [A-buffer algorithm](#12483-incremental-bubble-sort-a-buffer-blending.md) approach [S2, book].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **Performance:** The method is not real-time [S1]. Using 3 textures instead of a single one is about 2 to 3 times slower on recent GPUs [S1].
*   **Memory:** A huge amount of image data may not fit the graphics memory [S1].

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** Not real-time [S1]. Performance degrades with the number of texture layers; using 3 textures is 2-3x slower than 1 texture on recent GPUs [S1].
*   **Memory Complexity:** High. Large amounts of image data may exceed graphics memory capacity [S1].
*   **Strengths:** Allows extremely complex and extensive vegetation to be rendered in a reasonable time by leveraging precomputed data and hierarchical detail selection [S2, book].
*   **Limitations:** Not suitable for real-time applications [S1]. Limited by graphics memory capacity for large scenes [S1].
*   **When to use:** Offline rendering of complex vegetation where precomputation is feasible and real-time performance is not required [S1][S2, book].
*   **When not to use:** Real-time applications [S1].

## Background
The method was introduced by Max et al. in 1996 [S1][S2, book]. It is described in the context of rendering forest scenes [S1] and plane-parallel radiance transport for global illumination in vegetation [S2, book]. The approach builds on earlier work in image-based rendering and hierarchical modeling [S1][S2, book].
